subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The carpe diem tradition in love poetry, exemplified by Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress', urges the beloved to:
options: Seize the day and yield to love before time and death intervene
Wait patiently for marriage
Mourn a love already lost
Renounce earthly desire for spiritual love
questions.explain: Carpe diem means 'seize the day', pressing the beloved to act on desire because time is short.

questions.q: The concept of the 'male gaze', often applied in feminist re-readings of love poetry, draws attention to how:
options: The female beloved is frequently positioned as a passive object of male desire and viewing
Men were excluded from writing love poetry
Love poetry avoids describing women
Women poets dominated the love tradition
questions.explain: The male gaze frames the woman as the object to be looked at and desired, a perspective feminist critics interrogate.

questions.q: 'Forbidden' and 'transgressive' love in literature is often heightened by which contextual force?
options: A surplus of available wealth
Universal social approval of the match
The absence of any society at all
Rigid class, religious or familial codes the lovers defy
questions.explain: Transgressive love draws its charge from defying the social, religious or familial codes of its time.

questions.q: 'Courtly love', a medieval convention shaping later love poetry, characteristically presents the lover as:
options: A wealthy suitor negotiating a dowry
A humble servant devoted to an idealised, often unattainable lady
A rival seeking to humiliate the beloved
An indifferent master commanding his lady
questions.explain: Courtly love casts the male lover as a worshipful servant to a distant, idealised lady, often a married noblewoman.

questions.q: In the Petrarchan 'oxymoron' of love (e.g. 'icy fire', 'sweet pain'), the convention conveys love as:
options: A simple social duty
A wholly painless, untroubled state
A purely physical transaction
A paradoxical experience of contradictory feelings at once
questions.explain: The Petrarchan love-paradox yokes opposites to capture love's contradictory mix of pleasure and torment.

questions.q: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 ('My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun') is best read as:
options: An elegy for a dead lover
A carpe diem seduction poem
A satirical inversion of Petrarchan convention that nonetheless affirms real love
A sincere Petrarchan blazon of the beloved's perfection
questions.explain: Sonnet 130 mocks exaggerated Petrarchan praise while asserting a truer, unidealised love.

questions.q: The phrase 'love through the ages' invites study of how:
options: Only one definitive view of love exists for all time
Love poetry stopped being written after the Romantics
Conventions and representations of love evolve with shifting social and historical values
Context is irrelevant to love texts
questions.explain: The topic examines change and continuity in how love is represented across different periods.

questions.q: 'Forbidden love' as a theme typically generates dramatic tension because the lovers face:
options: An excess of public approval
Barriers of class, family, religion, law or social taboo
No obstacles at all
Only minor disagreements about taste
questions.explain: Forbidden love is heightened by external prohibitions of class, family, faith or law.

questions.q: Across the 'love through the ages' span, representations of marriage shift partly because:
options: Marriage was never a literary subject
Poets stopped writing about marriage entirely after 1600
All periods treated marriage identically
Marriage law and women's social/economic status changed over the centuries
questions.explain: Changing legal, economic and social conditions for women reshape how marriage is represented across periods.

questions.q: Comparing the treatment of love in a Renaissance and a twentieth-century text, a strong response would:
options: Show how each text's representation of love is shaped by its differing social and historical context
Ignore context entirely
Assume love means exactly the same thing in both periods
Rank the periods by which had better weather
questions.explain: Effective comparison links each representation of love to the values and conditions of its time.

questions.q: 'Unrequited love' as a convention denotes a love that is:
options: Purely spiritual and divine
Forbidden by law
Returned and fulfilled in marriage
Felt by one party but not returned by the other
questions.explain: Unrequited love is love that is not reciprocated, a long-standing source of lyric longing.

questions.q: The literary device known as the 'blazon' in love poetry refers to:
options: A poem renouncing love
A bitter complaint against marriage
An itemised catalogue praising the beloved's individual body parts
A pun on the lover's name
questions.explain: The blazon enumerates and praises the beloved's features in turn, central to Petrarchan idealisation.

questions.q: In love poetry, the 'complaint' or 'lament' tradition gives voice to:
options: A speaker grieving over rejection, absence or the cruelty of the beloved
A satirist mocking metre
A triumphant lover celebrating success
A neutral observer cataloguing weather
questions.explain: The amatory complaint expresses the suffering of the rejected, neglected or longing lover.

questions.q: The Renaissance 'cruel mistress' figure in love poetry functions to:
options: Withhold favour, prompting the lover's complaint and intensified longing
Narrate a battle scene
Reward the lover's devotion at once
Replace the speaker as the poem's voice
questions.explain: The cruel, withholding mistress generates the poetry of frustrated desire and complaint.

questions.q: In Andrew Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress', the argument's logical structure ('Had we but world enough... But... Now therefore') resembles:
options: A villanelle's refrain pattern
An elegy in four parts
A pastoral lullaby
A three-stage syllogistic seduction: if we had time, but we don't, therefore act now
questions.explain: The poem proceeds like a syllogism, moving from hypothetical leisure to the pressure of time to a 'therefore' urging action.

questions.q: Reading love poetry across the ages, a 'feminist' approach differs from a 'traditional' one chiefly by:
options: Refusing to read pre-1900 texts
Caring only about rhyme schemes
Treating all love poems as identical
Questioning the gendered power, voice and objectification the conventions encode
questions.explain: Feminist reading interrogates how love conventions encode and naturalise gendered power and the objectification of women.

questions.q: When a love poem's speaker idealises the beloved as flawless and almost divine, a critical reader should note that this:
options: Is unique to the twentieth century
Is a rhetorical convention that may reveal more about the lover's projection than the beloved's reality
Proves the beloved was a real saint
Means the poem cannot be analysed
questions.explain: Idealisation is a convention, and analysis should consider what the lover's projection reveals rather than taking it literally.

questions.q: Petrarchan idealisation of the beloved typically involves:
options: Refusal to describe the beloved at all
Mockery of the beloved's appearance
Realistic, unflattering physical description
Elaborate praise through hyperbolic conceits and a catalogue of perfect features
questions.explain: The Petrarchan mode idealises the beloved with hyperbole and the blazon, listing her perfect features.

questions.q: Christina Rossetti's love poetry is often read as complicating convention by:
options: Adopting an exclusively male speaker
Endorsing the carpe diem seduction without reservation
Avoiding the subject of love altogether
Foregrounding female restraint, renunciation or spiritual longing rather than easy fulfilment
questions.explain: Rossetti frequently voices ambivalence, restraint and spiritual yearning, resisting straightforward romantic resolution.

questions.q: Donne's 'The Sun Rising' treats love through which characteristic Metaphysical move?
options: A bold conceit in which the lovers' bedroom becomes the centre of the whole universe
A renunciation of physical desire
A simple pastoral celebration of shepherds
A modest, plain-spoken understatement
questions.explain: Donne hyperbolically argues the lovers contain everything, making their room the world's centre, a typical conceit.

questions.q: The tension between 'desire and duty' is a recurrent love-poetry concern in which a speaker:
options: Is torn between personal passion and social, moral or familial obligation
Feels no conflict whatsoever about love
Rejects both desire and duty for solitude
Is concerned only with rhyme
questions.explain: Many texts dramatise the clash between private desire and the demands of duty, honour or society.

questions.q: Across periods, the relationship between love and 'mutability' (change/transience) is a key concern because poets repeatedly confront:
options: The threat that time, ageing and death pose to love, prompting carpe diem or claims of poetic immortality
The irrelevance of time to love
The impossibility of writing about love
The permanence of all human feeling
questions.explain: Mutability drives both carpe diem urgency and the rival boast that verse can immortalise love beyond time.

questions.q: Shakespeare's claim in several sonnets that 'this' poem will outlast time and preserve the beloved illustrates the convention of:
options: The 'immortalising' power of poetry over death and decay
The cruel mistress
Carpe diem surrender
Courtly servitude
questions.explain: The immortalisation topos asserts that verse confers an enduring life on the beloved beyond mortal decay.

questions.q: A feminist re-reading of a Renaissance love sonnet would most likely emphasise:
options: The poet's exact birthplace
The poet's choice of rhyme scheme alone
The number of lines in the poem
How the woman is silenced or objectified, and whose voice and power the poem privileges
questions.explain: Feminist criticism foregrounds gendered power, voice and objectification within the text.

questions.q: A 'psychoanalytic' (Freudian) reading would typically attend to:
options: the economic base determining the cultural superstructure
the rhythm and metre of the verse alone
the unconscious, repression, desire and symbolic expressions of inner conflict
the text's fidelity to historical fact
questions.explain: Psychoanalytic criticism reads texts for unconscious drives, repression and symbolic enactments of psychic conflict.

questions.q: An 'unreliable narrator' is one whose:
options: narration is consistently omniscient and authoritative
story is told entirely in the present tense
perspective shifts between several characters
account the reader is invited to question because their credibility is compromised
questions.explain: An unreliable narrator's version of events is undermined by gaps, bias or self-deception that the reader must read against.

questions.q: A 'post-colonial' reading is most concerned with:
options: the purging of pity and fear in the audience
the recurrence of a single image
metre and rhyme scheme
representations of empire, the colonised 'other', hybridity and cultural power
questions.explain: Post-colonial criticism interrogates how texts construct empire, the colonised subject and relations of cultural power.

questions.q: A 'reader-response' approach holds that meaning is:
options: fixed entirely by the author's stated intention
irrelevant to literary study
determined solely by the historical context of composition
produced in the interaction between the text and the reader's act of interpretation
questions.explain: Reader-response criticism locates meaning in the transaction between text and reader rather than in the author alone.

questions.q: When two texts are compared, a 'point of divergence' is most valuable when it:
options: shows the texts are completely unrelated
proves one text is superior
reveals how each writer handles a shared concern differently, illuminating both
repeats a similarity already noted
questions.explain: Productive comparison uses difference to sharpen understanding of each text's distinctive method and meaning.

questions.q: In a comparative essay, the strongest approach to comparison is to:
options: build an integrated argument in which texts are set against each other around shared concerns and differing methods
summarise text one fully, then text two, with no cross-reference
compare the authors' biographies in detail
note only that the texts share a theme
questions.explain: High-level comparison interweaves texts around a thesis, analysing similarities and differences in method and effect.
